Your agent can help you understand a database, prepare a schema change, and
follow it as it runs. How you give it access matters:

- **With its own account**, give it read-only access to inspect schemas and
  follow changes. The [authentication guide](auth.md#calling-schemabot-as-a-service)
  explains how to set this up.
- **With your account**, its actions are recorded as yours. If it runs the CLI
  with your credentials or posts a comment from your GitHub account, SchemaBot
  cannot tell whether you or your agent sent the command.

The guidance below is a cautious starting point you can adapt for your team.
It includes instructions you can give your agent and settings you can enforce
on the server.

## You decide what runs in production

Let your agent prepare the change and explain what will happen. Under the
policy below, you run the production command yourself. That keeps the final
decision with you and makes the recorded action match who took it.

PR approval is a separate check. Where the review gate is enabled, SchemaBot
requires approval before applying a change. That check still applies
when an agent sends the command, but it cannot tell whether you reviewed what
your agent is about to do with your credentials.

## Decide when your agent should ask

| Task | Suggested boundary |
|---|---|
| Run a production command such as `apply`, `apply-confirm`, `cutover`, or `rollback` | You run it yourself, even if you previously asked the agent to do it |
| Run a command with `--allow-unsafe`, in any environment | You review the destructive change and run the command yourself |
| Apply to a shared staging database or one that other teams depend on | Your agent asks first |
| Apply to a new or isolated staging database with little impact on others | Your agent explains what it will do, then proceeds |
| Apply when it is unclear who depends on the database | Your agent asks first |
| Inspect status, progress, history, a stored plan, or the live schema | Your agent can use its read access without asking each time |

If you prefer to run every write command yourself, say so in your agent's
instructions. That takes precedence over the staging defaults above.

Staging changes can affect other people too. A change can disrupt their tests
or hold a database lock while it runs. Use your team's service criticality
ratings if you have them; otherwise, ask before changing any shared staging
database. Any configured approval requirements still apply.

## Give your agent clear instructions

You can copy this into your agent's instructions:

> - Prepare production commands for me to review and run. Do not execute them,
>   even if I ask you to.
> - Do not run commands with `--allow-unsafe`. Show me the change and the exact
>   command so I can decide and run it myself.
> - Before applying to staging, check who depends on the database. Ask me first
>   if it is shared, critical, or unclear. For a new or isolated database with
>   little impact on others, explain what you will do before proceeding.
> - If I say I will run all write commands myself, follow that preference.
> - Use your read access to inspect status, progress, stored plans, history,
>   and live schemas. Creating a new plan requires write access.
> - If a request returns `403`, explain the missing permission. Do not try other
>   credentials or disable authentication to get around it. Ask an operator to
>   check whether the account should have access.
> - Propose schema changes by editing the schema files in a pull request, where
>   I can review the plan and follow the checks.

## Back it up with server settings

Instructions guide your agent. Server settings control what it can do with
the credentials you give it. They cannot make an action “human only” when
the agent uses your credentials.

- **Give services their own read-only access.** The `forward_auth` service lane
  limits listed SPIFFE identities to reads. With OIDC, keep admin groups out
  of service tokens: a token with an admin group can write, even when it
  belongs to a service. See [service access](auth.md#calling-schemabot-as-a-service).
- **Choose which accounts can run PR commands.** Enable
  `pr_command_authorization` and leave bot accounts out of admin and operator
  grants when you want them to remain read-only. Check repository-level admin
  grants too. See [GitHub permissions](auth.md#github-side-authorization).
- **Require review before apply.** Enable
  [`review_policy`](configuration.md#review-gate) to require a qualifying
  approval for the environments served by that instance. The PR author's
  own approval does not count.
- **Review destructive changes before allowing them.** Changes flagged as unsafe
  require `--allow-unsafe` to proceed. If your agent uses your credentials, it
  can supply that flag too—SchemaBot cannot tell whether you personally
  approved the change.
- **Check the logs when a command is denied.** They explain why it was blocked
  and help you check the caller's permissions. The
  `schemabot.pr_command_actor_authorization.total` metric can help you spot
  patterns across requests.
